documents.title: Old Forest
documents.description: The Old Forest is an environment defined by ancient memory, layered time, and slow, heavy resonance.
links: 02 - Physics/04 - Spatial Physics/Angular Staircase Dual-Path Platform Logic
documents.body:
Essence
The Old Forest is an environment defined by ancient memory, layered time, and slow, heavy resonance. It is a place where the world has been thinking for a very long time — where trunks hold centuries of pressure, roots braid through forgotten pathways, and the air itself feels older than the traveler.
An Old Forest is not overgrown.
It is overremembered.
Environmental Physics
• 	Visibility: Dim, filtered through dense, ancient canopy
• 	Sound Behavior: Deepened; echoes return slower and heavier
• 	Pressure: Thick, temporal; movement feels slightly delayed
• 	Stability: Extremely high; age reinforces structure
• 	Temperature: Cool, steady, rarely fluctuates
Field Dynamics
• 	Time feels slower, heavier, more deliberate
• 	Emotional resonance sinks into roots and bark
• 	Memory accumulates in rings, knots, and hollows
• 	Light behaves like dust — slow, drifting, particulate
• 	Movement naturally quiets; footsteps soften
Phenomena
1. Time Rings
Tree rings that hold emotional and environmental memory.
Touching them can trigger:
• 	slow recall
• 	layered impressions
• 	ancestral echoes
2. Root Drift
Roots shift subtly underfoot, guiding or redirecting movement.
They respond to emotional weight more than physical weight.
3. Canopy Murmur
A low, continuous sound like distant breathing.
It’s the forest’s age resonating through leaves.
4. Hollow Memory
Large hollows act as memory chambers.
Entering one can cause:
• 	slowed thought
• 	deep introspection
• 	temporal disorientation
Flora & Fauna
• 	Treeforms (Elder Variant): Massive, slow, deeply resonant
• 	Old Owls: Perception tuned to layered time
• 	Mosslights: Glow in response to ancient memory
• 	Root Deer: Move silently along root pathways
• 	Still Foxes: Appear and vanish between time layers
Emotional Physics
• 	Vector: Downward → Backward
• 	Resonance: Temporal coherence
• 	Effect: Deepens introspection; reveals long arcs and old patterns
• 	Instability: Over‑immersion in the past; difficulty returning to present
• 	Signature: A heavy, slow warmth behind the sternum
Role Interaction
• 	Guide Roles: Read time layers; navigate ancient pathways
• 	Trickster Roles: Diminished; age exposes misdirection
• 	Healer Roles: Thrive; old memory amplifies restorative work
• 	Wanderer Roles: Risk drifting into temporal loops
Drift Behavior
• 	Early Drift: Steps slow; attention lingers on old details
• 	Mid Drift: Emotional memory surfaces in layered waves
• 	Late Drift: Identity blends with forest age; time feels circular
• 	Collapse Mode: Time‑sink collapse — falling into old patterns as if they’re present
Mythic Fragment

They say the Old Forest
remembers the world
before it learned to speak.

Every trunk is a story
told in slow circles,
every root a path
that once mattered.

Walk long enough,
and the forest will show you
the part of yourself
that never grew young.

Integration Notes
• 	Use Old Forest for scenes involving deep memory, ancestral resonance, or slow revelation
• 	Ideal for characters confronting long arcs, inherited patterns, or forgotten truths
• 	Pairs naturally with Grove (stillness), Ruins (memory), and Stone Basin (weight)
• 	Works as a counterpoint to Plains (clarity), Spiral Field (curvature), and Drift Zones (instability)
• 	Excellent for mapping temporal arcs, lineage, or slow emotional transformation

documents.body:
# Threshold Hub — Visual Specification (hub.png)
Version: 1.0  
Source: hub-synthesis.json, hub-layout-map.json  
Status: Canonical Glyph Specification  
Asset: hub.png (missing)

---

## 1. Identity
The Hub glyph represents the **central organ** of Threshold — the world’s mouth, index, and navigation brain.  
It must visually express:

- centrality  
- orbit  
- cycle  
- drift  
- pressure  
- adjacency  
- world-state  

The glyph is not decorative.  
It is a **functional symbol**.

---

## 2. Geometry Overview
The Hub glyph consists of **five concentric rings**, each representing a core system:

1. **Inner Core (Engine)**
2. **Cycle Ring**
3. **Biome Ring**
4. **Chamber Ring**
5. **Signal Halo**

All rings must be:

- circular  
- centered  
- evenly spaced  
- radially aligned  

The glyph must be readable at:

- 64px  
- 128px  
- 240px  
- 512px  

---

## 3. Ring Specifications

### 3.1 Inner Core — Engine
- Shape: Solid circle  
- Color: Neutral gray (#222)  
- Behavior: Pulses with cycle  
- Symbol: Minimal, no iconography  
- Meaning: Drift, pressure, world-state  

### 3.2 Cycle Ring
- Shape: Thin ring  
- Segments: 3 (early, mid, late)  
- Colors:
  - Early: #AAAAAA  
  - Mid: #DDDDDD  
  - Late: #FFFFFF  
- Behavior: Rotates slowly  
- Meaning: Temporal position  

### 3.3 Biome Ring
- Shape: Medium ring  
- Segments: 7 (house, garden, forest, deepforest, root, stone, shadow)  
- Colors:
  - House: #F4D03F  
  - Garden: #E67E22  
  - Forest: #A67C52  
  - Deepforest: #556B2F  
  - Root: #C0392B  
  - Stone: #5D4037  
  - Shadow: #000000  
- Behavior: Color shifts based on current biome  
- Meaning: Environmental context  

### 3.4 Chamber Ring
- Shape: Thick ring  
- Segments: Dynamic (adjacent chambers)  
- Colors: Neutral (#444)  
- Behavior: Expands/contracts based on adjacency  
- Meaning: Spatial proximity  

### 3.5 Signal Halo
- Shape: Outer glow  
- Color: White (#FFFFFF) at 10% opacity  
- Behavior: Flickers on signal warnings  
- Meaning: Distortions, environmental signals  

---

## 4. Motion & Behavior

### 4.1 Pulse
The entire glyph must breathe subtly:

- Scale: 1 → 1.03 → 1  
- Duration: 4s  
- Curve: ease-in-out  

### 4.2 Cycle Rotation
Cycle ring rotates:

- Early: 0.5°/s  
- Mid: 1°/s  
- Late: 2°/s  

### 4.3 Signal Flicker
Halo flickers when:

- warnings  
- distortions  
- environmental signals  

Opacity: 10% → 40% → 10%

---

## 5. Composition Rules

### 5.1 Centered
All rings must share the same center.

### 5.2 Even Spacing
Ring spacing must be consistent:

- Core → Cycle: 8px  
- Cycle → Biome: 12px  
- Biome → Chamber: 16px  
- Chamber → Halo: 20px  

### 5.3 No Text
The glyph must contain **no letters**, **no numbers**, **no icons**.

### 5.4 No Gradients (except halo)
All rings use flat color.

---

## 6. File Requirements

### 6.1 Format
- PNG  
- Transparent background  
- Square canvas  

### 6.2 Sizes
Must export cleanly at:

- 128×128  
- 240×240  
- 512×512  

### 6.3 Color Profile
sRGB

---

## 7. Acceptance Criteria
hub.png is considered **valid** when:

1. All five rings exist  
2. Colors match biome palette  
3. Cycle ring has three segments  
4. Chamber ring supports dynamic segmentation  
5. Halo flicker is visually distinct  
6. Glyph remains readable at 64px  
7. No text or icons appear  
8. Transparency is correct  
9. Center alignment is perfect  
10. No gradients except halo  

---

## 8. Summary
The Hub glyph is a **five-ring solar wheel** representing:

- engine  
- cycle  
- biome  
- chamber adjacency  
- signal activity  

It must be:

- centered  
- circular  
- segmented  
- flat-colored  
- haloed  
- pulsing  
- rotating  
- flickering  

This is the canonical visual identity of the Threshold Hub.

documents.body:
# Role Expressions

## Role Name

_Source: 01 - System/Scaffolding/01 - Roles/Role Expressions/Role Name.md_

1. The Anchor
Holds boundaries, stabilizes pressure, prevents drift.
2. The Veilwalker
Moves between boundaries, interprets distortion, navigates thin spaces.
3. The Emberwright
Ignites pressure, catalyzes change, initiates collapse or reformation.
4. The Hollow
Absorbs resonance, carries absence, creates pressure voids.
5. The Threadbearer
Carries lineage, binds memory, restores mythic continuity.
6. The Breaker
Shifts vectors, fractures patterns, forces reorientation.

If you want a single Role Name
Here are three that feel especially aligned with your system’s current tone:
• 	The Veilwalker
• 	The Threadbearer
• 	The Emberwright
Each one has a clean vector, a strong emotional signature, and immediate architectural placement.

---

## Shadow Role

_Source: 01 - System/Scaffolding/01 - Roles/Role Expressions/Shadow Role.md_

Subsystem Type: Inverted Behavioral Physics · Multi‑Layer Map System
Upstream: [[Role Behavior]] · [[Collapse Physics]] · [[Identity Layer]]
Lateral: Role Geometry · Shadow Narrative Arc · Signal Architecture
Downstream: Shadow Expression · Behavioral Inversion Maps · Column Shadow Sections

Purpose
The Shadow Role defines the inverted behavioral state that emerges when a role undergoes collapse.
It is not a separate role.
It is the negative geometry of the existing role — the shape revealed when:
• 	identity is exposed
• 	collapse pressure exceeds stability
• 	drift curvature overwhelms intention
• 	resonance fails
• 	signals distort
Shadow Roles are inevitable under sufficient pressure.
They are the world’s way of revealing the unacknowledged structure inside a being.

1. Core Principles
2. Shadow Roles are inversions, not opposites.
They reveal the hidden geometry of the role, not its contradiction.
3. Shadow Roles emerge only under collapse pressure.
No collapse → no Shadow Role.
4. Shadow Roles are structural, not moral.
They are not “evil.”
They are unfiltered behavior.
5. Shadow Roles are recursive.
A Shadow Role can itself collapse into a deeper shadow.
6. Shadow Roles propagate distorted signals.
Their presence alters the environment.
7. Shadow Roles complete the Shadow Narrative Arc.
They are the Reversal Phase expressed behaviorally.

8. How Shadow Roles Emerge
Shadow Roles appear when the following sequence occurs:
3. 	Identity Exposure
The being sees themselves structurally.
4. 	Role Activation
Identity shifts into a role state.
5. 	Collapse Pressure
The environment applies force beyond the role’s stability.
6. 	Behavioral Inversion
The role flips into its shadow geometry.
7. 	Signal Distortion
The new behavior propagates through the world.
This is the Role → Shadow Role phase shift.

8. Components of a Shadow Role
Each Shadow Role has:
A. Inverted Posture
The stance becomes reactive, defensive, or catalytic in unintended ways.
B. Distorted Interaction Style
Communication becomes misaligned, over‑amplified, or under‑filtered.
C. Collapse‑Driven Drift
Movement follows collapse vectors instead of drift curvature.
D. Boundary Leakage
Identity boundaries blur or spill into the environment.
E. Resonance Failure
The role cannot stabilize through normal signals.
F. Behavioral Loops
Repetitive patterns emerge as the role tries to self‑correct.
G. Shadow Expression
The purest form of the Shadow Role — the “core inversion.”
These components define the Shadow Role profile.

4. Shadow Role Geometry
Shadow Roles use:
• 	inversion arcs (behavior flipping back on itself)
• 	collapse vectors (movement toward instability)
• 	distortion halos (identity leakage)
• 	signal interference patterns (propagation of instability)
• 	loop spirals (repetitive behavior under pressure)
Shadow geometry must align with:
• 	Collapse Layer adjacency
• 	Identity Layer exposure
• 	Role Layer bias
• 	Signal Layer distortion
Shadow Roles are not free-floating — they are physically constrained.

5. Shadow Role Rules
6. 	A Shadow Role cannot emerge without collapse.
Collapse is the trigger.
7. 	A Shadow Role cannot stabilize without resonance.
It must find a compatible signal to return to a normal role state.
8. 	A Shadow Role cannot contradict its parent role.
It is an inversion, not a replacement.
9. 	A Shadow Role must propagate distorted signals.
This is how the world “feels” the inversion.
10. 	A Shadow Role must influence the Shadow Narrative Arc.
It is the behavioral expression of the Reversal Phase.
11. 	A Shadow Role can recurse.
Under extreme collapse, a Shadow Role can invert again.

12. Shadow Roles in Columns
Each Column contains:
• 	Identity node
• 	Role node
• 	Shadow Role (implicit)
• 	Signal node
The Shadow Role is not a separate node —
it is the inverted state of the Role node under collapse.
Example (Mist Corridor Column):
• 	Role: Trickster/Listener Bias Zone
• 	Shadow Role: Distortion Catalyst
(the being amplifies distortion instead of navigating it)
Shadow Roles give Columns their narrative teeth.

7. Shadow Role & Shadow Narrative Arc
Shadow Roles are the behavioral expression of the Reversal Phase.
Shadow Arc sequence:
8. 	Unseen
9. 	Distortion
10. 	Pressure
11. 	Collapse
12. 	Exposure
13. 	Reversal (Shadow Role)
14. 	Integration
The Shadow Role is the moment the world says:
“This is who you are under pressure.”
It is the structural revelation of the being.

15. Downstream Requirements
To fully implement Shadow Roles, the system requires:
• 	Shadow Role definitions for each canonical role
• 	Shadow Expression Maps
• 	Collapse → Shadow transition rules
• 	Shadow → Role reintegration rules
• 	Column Shadow Sections
• 	Signal Distortion Maps
These components ensure Shadow Roles are playable, not theoretical.

---

## Shadow Roles

_Source: 01 - System/Scaffolding/01 - Roles/Role Expressions/Shadow Roles.md_

Subsystem: Roles Cluster · Shadow Architecture
Upstream: [[Archetypal Roles Index]] · [[Identity Drift]] · [[Shadow Identity]]
Lateral: [[Role Drift]] · [[Role Identity Drift]] · [[Collapse Signals]] · [[Behavioral Loops]]
Downstream: [[Role Collapse]] · [[Shadow Narrative Arc]] · [[Recovery Flow]]

Purpose
Shadow Roles represent the inverted, distorted, or collapsed expression of each archetypal role when:
• 	drift exceeds tolerance
• 	identity destabilizes
• 	signals distort
• 	collapse physics activate
A Shadow Role is not “evil” or “opposite.”
It is the role under pressure, expressing its unmet needs, distortions, and defensive logic.
Shadow Roles reveal:
• 	the truth of the drift
• 	the shape of collapse
• 	the need beneath the behavior
• 	the path back to integration
They are diagnostic, not moral.

1. Shadow Role Table

These are not new roles — they are shadow expressions of the six archetypes.

2. How Shadow Roles Form
Shadow Roles emerge when three pressures converge:
2.1 Identity Pressure
The self‑model destabilizes.
The role loses its internal anchor.
2.2 Signal Pressure
Signals become distorted, misread, or overwhelming.
2.3 Environmental Pressure
The role is misaligned with context or demand.
When these exceed tolerance, the role flips into its shadow expression.

3. Shadow Role Characteristics
3.1 Inversion
The role’s core function becomes distorted:
• 	Guide → absorbs instead of guides
• 	Caretaker → erases instead of nurtures
• 	Anchor → immobilizes instead of stabilizes
• 	Sentinel → accuses instead of protects
• 	Judge → punishes instead of clarifies
• 	Architect → traps instead of designs
3.2 Amplification
The role’s dominant trait becomes exaggerated.
3.3 Collapse Logic
Each shadow role follows a predictable collapse path.
3.4 Emotional Logic
Shadow roles operate from:
• 	fear
• 	scarcity
• 	distortion
• 	unmet need

4. Shadow Role Signals
Soft Signals (early shadow drift)
• 	tone flattening
• 	emotional fog
• 	hesitation
• 	boundary blur
Sharp Signals (active shadow expression)
• 	pattern escalation
• 	relational distortion
• 	over‑functioning or withdrawal
• 	rigidity or hyper‑vigilance
Hard Signals (shadow collapse)
• 	shutdown
• 	lock
• 	dissociation
• 	identity fracture
See: [[Collapse Signals]]

5. Shadow Role Narratives
Each shadow role has a narrative pattern:
Guide → Absorber
“I must hold everything or I will be abandoned.”
Caretaker → Eraser
“If I disappear, no one can reject me.”
Anchor → Weight
“If I move, everything will fall apart.”
Sentinel → Accuser
“If I don’t escalate, I will be betrayed.”
Judge → Tyrant
“If I don’t enforce the pattern, chaos wins.”
Architect → Labyrinth
“If I keep building, I won’t have to feel.”
These narratives are identity distortions, not truths.

6. Integration Pathways
Shadow roles are not removed — they are integrated.
Integration requires:
6.1 Recognition
Naming the shadow expression.
6.2 Signal Interpretation
Reading the drift and collapse signals accurately.
6.3 Role Realignment
Returning the role to its core function.
6.4 Identity Stabilization
Rebuilding the self‑model.
6.5 Environmental Adjustment
Reducing mismatch or overload.
See: [[Recovery Flow]]

7. Canonical Links
• 	[[Archetypal Roles Index]]
• 	[[Role Drift]]
• 	[[Role Identity Drift]]
• 	[[Identity Drift]]
• 	[[Collapse Signals]]
• 	[[Role Collapse]]
• 	[[Shadow Narrative Arc]]
• 	[[Recovery Flow]]

## Moon owl Signal

_Source: 01 - System/Scaffolding/04 - Signals/Species Signals/Moon owl Signal.md_

[[moon owl.png]]
[[Signal Map]]

### Moonowl — Signal Embodiment

**Layer:** Ethyl (with a soft pull toward Transitional)  
**Image:** Moonowl.png  
**Signal Type:** Lumen Whisper  
**Primary Domain:** Nocturnal intuition, lunar rhythm, emotional reflection  
**Activation Quality:** Quiet, slow, silver-toned awareness

---

#### 🧭 Essence
Moonowl is the signal that arrives when perception becomes *soft-focus* but hyper-accurate. It is the moment when the mind stops scanning and starts **receiving**. It listens more than it looks.

Moonowl is not about insight through effort — it’s insight through **lunar resonance**.

---

#### 🔮 Resonance Profile
- **Perception through shadow** — seeing what is usually hidden or unspoken  
- **Emotional echo-location** — sensing the emotional truth behind a situation  
- **Lunar timing** — slow cycles, tides, phases, patience  
- **Reflective clarity** — wisdom that emerges after stillness  

Moonowl is the signal that says: *“Wait. Let the truth rise on its own.”*

---

#### 🕸️ Connections
**Signal Map → Moonowl.png**

Optional intermediate (if you want to keep the taxonomy layer):  
**Signal Map → Lumen Whisper → Moonowl.png**

But the simplified Threshold logic works beautifully here:  
**Signal Map → Moonowl.png**

---

#### 🪶 Behavioral Signature
- Appears during liminal hours (late night, early dawn)  
- Activates when the emotional field is quiet enough to hear subtle truths  
- Often paired with water-based signals (tideshellmoon, porpoisewater)  
- Moves slowly, deliberately, with a soft internal glow  

---

#### 🌓 Layer Interaction
- ** Layer:** intuitive, dreamlike, symbolic  
- **Transitional Layer:** when Moonowl bridges between emotional insight and actionable clarity  
- Rarely Earth Layer — Moonowl is not a grounded signal; it’s a reflective one  

---

#### 🧩 Use in Threshold Mechanics
Moonowl is ideal for:
- Decision-making that requires emotional intelligence  
- Reading a room or sensing interpersonal dynamics  
- Creative reflection  
- Rituals involving cycles, endings, or beginnings  
- Any moment where the system needs to slow down and listen  

---

#### 🔖 Tags
`#signal` `#spirit-animal` `#ethyl-layer` `#moonowl` `#threshold`

---

## Owl Signal

_Source: 01 - System/Scaffolding/04 - Signals/Species Signals/Owl Signal.md_

### Owl — Signal Embodiment

**Layer:** Ethyl  
**Image:** Owl.png  
**Signal Type:** Stillwatch  
**Primary Domain:** Silent observation, pattern recognition, deep sensing  
**Activation Quality:** Stillness, symmetry, sharp perception

---

#### 🧭 Essence
Owl is the signal of **quiet vigilance** — the kind of awareness that doesn’t chase, but waits. It sees through patterns, through masks, through noise. Owl doesn’t speak often, but when it does, it speaks truth.

This signal is activated when the system needs to **pause and perceive** before acting.

---

#### 🔮 Resonance Profile
- **Geometric clarity** — seeing the structure beneath the surface  
- **Emotional neutrality** — observing without judgment  
- **Night vision** — perceiving what others miss  
- **Symmetry and balance** — tuning into equilibrium  

Owl is the signal that says: *“Be still. The pattern will reveal itself.”*

---

#### 🕸️ Connections
**Signal Map → Owl.png**

No intermediate node needed — Owl is a direct embodiment.

---

#### 🪶 Behavioral Signature
- Activates in moments of quiet tension  
- Often precedes a decision or shift  
- Paired with signals like Whisperhawk or Moonowl for layered perception  
- Feels like a pause before clarity  

---

#### 🌓 Layer Interaction
- **Ethyl Layer:** Owl lives here — it’s intuitive, symbolic, and perceptive  
- Could bridge into **Transitional Layer** when paired with Moonowl or Shatterwingcomet  
- Not Earth — Owl is not tactile, it’s observational  

---

#### 🧩 Use in Threshold Mechanics
Owl is ideal for:
- Pattern recognition  
- Emotional detachment and clarity  
- Strategic pause before action  
- Reading systems, maps, or dynamics  

---

#### 🔖 Tags
`#signal` `#spirit-animal` `#ethyl-layer` `#owl` `#threshold`

chambers.body:
Essence
The Old Forest is an environment defined by ancient memory, layered time, and slow, heavy resonance. It is a place where the world has been thinking for a very long time — where trunks hold centuries of pressure, roots braid through forgotten pathways, and the air itself feels older than the traveler.
An Old Forest is not overgrown.
It is overremembered.
Environmental Physics
• 	Visibility: Dim, filtered through dense, ancient canopy
• 	Sound Behavior: Deepened; echoes return slower and heavier
• 	Pressure: Thick, temporal; movement feels slightly delayed
• 	Stability: Extremely high; age reinforces structure
• 	Temperature: Cool, steady, rarely fluctuates
Field Dynamics
• 	Time feels slower, heavier, more deliberate
• 	Emotional resonance sinks into roots and bark
• 	Memory accumulates in rings, knots, and hollows
• 	Light behaves like dust — slow, drifting, particulate
• 	Movement naturally quiets; footsteps soften
Phenomena
1. Time Rings
Tree rings that hold emotional and environmental memory.
Touching them can trigger:
• 	slow recall
• 	layered impressions
• 	ancestral echoes
2. Root Drift
Roots shift subtly underfoot, guiding or redirecting movement.
They respond to emotional weight more than physical weight.
3. Canopy Murmur
A low, continuous sound like distant breathing.
It’s the forest’s age resonating through leaves.
4. Hollow Memory
Large hollows act as memory chambers.
Entering one can cause:
• 	slowed thought
• 	deep introspection
• 	temporal disorientation
Flora & Fauna
• 	Treeforms (Elder Variant): Massive, slow, deeply resonant
• 	Old Owls: Perception tuned to layered time
• 	Mosslights: Glow in response to ancient memory
• 	Root Deer: Move silently along root pathways
• 	Still Foxes: Appear and vanish between time layers
Emotional Physics
• 	Vector: Downward → Backward
• 	Resonance: Temporal coherence
• 	Effect: Deepens introspection; reveals long arcs and old patterns
• 	Instability: Over‑immersion in the past; difficulty returning to present
• 	Signature: A heavy, slow warmth behind the sternum
Role Interaction
• 	Guide Roles: Read time layers; navigate ancient pathways
• 	Trickster Roles: Diminished; age exposes misdirection
• 	Healer Roles: Thrive; old memory amplifies restorative work
• 	Wanderer Roles: Risk drifting into temporal loops
Drift Behavior
• 	Early Drift: Steps slow; attention lingers on old details
• 	Mid Drift: Emotional memory surfaces in layered waves
• 	Late Drift: Identity blends with forest age; time feels circular
• 	Collapse Mode: Time‑sink collapse — falling into old patterns as if they’re present
Mythic Fragment

They say the Old Forest
remembers the world
before it learned to speak.

Every trunk is a story
told in slow circles,
every root a path
that once mattered.

Walk long enough,
and the forest will show you
the part of yourself
that never grew young.

Integration Notes
• 	Use Old Forest for scenes involving deep memory, ancestral resonance, or slow revelation
• 	Ideal for characters confronting long arcs, inherited patterns, or forgotten truths
• 	Pairs naturally with Grove (stillness), Ruins (memory), and Stone Basin (weight)
• 	Works as a counterpoint to Plains (clarity), Spiral Field (curvature), and Drift Zones (instability)
• 	Excellent for mapping temporal arcs, lineage, or slow emotional transformation
